newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Gaps emerge in US, Vietnam views on ties.
newsitem.headline: Gaps emerge in US, Vietnam views on ties.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin hailed the signing on Monday of a debt rescheduling pact with Vietnam as a significant step, but said it would take time for the two wartime enemies to forge closer economic ties.

Rubin, the highest ranking U.S. economic official to visit here since the war ended in 1975, urged Hanoi to press ahead with its market reforms, saying that was the way for it to win trade concessions and financing from Washington.
But Vietnamese officials responded to Rubin's comments, made at a business seminar, with frustration.

Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, considered a champion of Hanoi's reform process, said Washington, and not Hanoi, was responsible for the slow progress in relations since diplomatic ties between the wartime foes were normalised nearly two years ago.
"Vietnam seriously recognises that the reason for that is not caused by the Vietnamese side," Kiet was quoted as saying by the official Vietnam News Agency during a meeting with Rubin.

Kiet said he believed the problems would be overcome, but added that Vietnam's legal environment was already developed to the point where American and other foreign investors could do business with reaonable confidence.
In a separate speech, Deputy Foreign Minister Nguyen Dinh Bin stressed the point further, saying there was a limit to what Hanoi should be expected to do on its own.
"It would be unfair to set forth requirements beyond Vietnam's real ability and higher than those for other countries," Bin said.
"We...hope that the United States will take more positive measures to speed up this (economic normalisation) process."

The two countries cleared a hurdle to broaden economic ties with their signing of the agreement to reschedule $145 million in debts that Hanoi inherited from the U.S.-backed Saigon government after the Vietnam War.
Under the pact, Hanoi was given until 2019 to repay the four development loans and two food credits incurred by its former enemy in the south.
"This agreement removes an important obstacle to closer ties between the United States and Vietnam," Rubin said. "This is a significant step."
The Treasury chief, who held separate a separate meeting with Finance Minister Nguyen Sinh Hung, said his visit signified a shift in the relationship from conflict to cooperation.

The next step is a trade agreement between the two countries. But for that to come about, Vietnam must make substantial commitments to open up its markets and treat foreign companies the same as Vietnamese ones, he said.

A trade deal is one condition needed for communist Vietnam to earn Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status from the United States. MFN, which guarantees non-discriminatory tariffs on exports, would give Vietnam access to the world's largest consumer market.

Rubin told reporters he had discussed MFN in meetings with Kiet and Hung, but had not focused on the question of when it would be granted. The two sides are scheduled to resume negotiations next week.
"These things by their nature take time," he said. "They are complicated."
He said Vietnam, which began experimenting with economic reforms more than a decade ago, had made great strides but that further progress on opening its market would inevitably be slow.
Rubin's visit is part of the sometimes painstaking process of mending relations. The United States normalised diplomatic ties with Vietnam only in mid-1995.
